messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 48, Michael, a married shopowner in a North American working-class suburb, still found that certain ordinary moments could pull him back into the night his younger brother died. The trauma had not been something he witnessed in the abstract but something intimate and brutal: his brother had been struck and killed in a sudden roadside crash after leaving Michael’s store, and Michael had been the one who got the call, drove to the scene, and stood helplessly near the covered body while police and bystanders moved around him. In the months that followed, funerals, cemeteries, and even casual conversations about people losing loved ones became difficult to tolerate. He would hear a customer mention a parent’s death or see a funeral procession go by the shop windows and feel a hard drop in his stomach, as though grief itself were about to walk through the door. He began changing the subject, stepping outside for a smoke, or finding any excuse not to think about it. He told himself that if he let the memory in, he would be flooded by the same horror and guilt he felt that night, and smoking became one of the few things that gave his hands something to do when the images threatened to rise. But the more he kept the event at a distance, the more it seemed to stay lodged in him untouched, and when it surfaced it arrived with the same sharp detail, as if all that effort not to think about it had kept the memory close and intact.

What made those reminders so powerful was how the memory continued to behave inside him. Michael did not describe the event as something finished; he said it felt as if it were happening again, with a vividness that was almost unbearable. That sense of danger kept pulling him back toward the crash, as if he had to keep revisiting it in his mind to stay ahead of whatever might happen next, and on the nights when he felt most on guard the scene came back most forcefully, fully formed before he could stop it. He could see the streetlights, the position of the car, the flash of emergency lights, and the exact angle of his brother’s body bag with such clarity that it played in his mind like a film he could not stop. When those images came, he would deliberately push them away, refusing to think about the event and turning instead to cigarettes, work paperwork, or anything that could keep him from standing still with the memory. Yet the more he tried to avoid it, the more fixed the scene became. He noticed that after a few minutes of trying not to think, the details returned sharper, as if the act of blocking them out only made the replay more intense.

Over time, his sense of danger also changed the way he moved through everyday life. Ordinary sounds made him jump; a dropped box in the shop or the sudden clang of the back door would send a jolt through him that felt out of proportion to the moment. Unexpected movement nearby was even worse. If a customer reached quickly toward a shelf or someone came up behind him without warning, he reacted as if he were in immediate danger, shoulders tensing and heart racing before he could tell himself where he was. Those reactions left him on edge, and the more keyed up he felt, the more he reached for cigarettes to steady himself. Smoking became part of his daily rhythm at the shop, something he did in the alley between customers or in the car before going home, because he believed he needed it to calm the surges of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame that came with the memory and with his jumpy body. But the cigarettes did not simply soothe him; they also gave him more chances to slip away from thinking about his brother, from grief-related events, and from the people who reminded him of loss. He stopped attending funerals, avoided cemeteries, and made polite but quick exits whenever a conversation turned toward death. He even found himself avoiding customers or acquaintances who reminded him of someone he had lost, which narrowed his world and left the shop feeling both safer and lonelier.

At the same time, the constant effort not to feel or remember seemed to keep the fear alive. Because he was always bracing for sounds, movements, or reminders of loss, he became more alert to them in the first place. A person entering the store too quickly, a siren outside, or a funeral notice in the paper could all set him off, and once activated he was right back in the scene of the crash, reliving it with the same vivid detail and conviction that it was happening now. Michael had come to see himself as someone who had to stay guarded at all times, but that vigilance was exhausting and reinforced his belief that danger was never far away. By the time he sought help, it was because the cycle had begun to affect his marriage and his work: his wife noticed how often he was outside smoking, how rarely he could stay present during family conversations, and how much effort it took for him to get through a day in the shop without feeling overwhelmed. He finally came in hoping to get some control back, but what frightened him most was that the memory would keep ambushing him forever, and what he hoped for, more than anything, was to be able to think of his brother without the night of the crash rushing back as if no time had passed at all.
